Yes, it is possible. Below is an explicit construction.

**Choice of parameter.** Pick any $p\in(0,1)\setminus\{1/2\}$; for definiteness take $p=1/3$. We will build a partition $X,Y$ of $\mathbb R$ with both sets dense in every non-empty open interval and with
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\lambda(X\cap[-t,t])}{2t}=p,\qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\lambda(Y\cap[-t,t])}{2t}=1-p.$$

**Step 1 — a periodic "fat" open dense set.** For each integer $n$, let $C_n\subset(n,n+1)$ be a fat Cantor set: closed, nowhere dense in $(n,n+1)$, with $\lambda(C_n)=1-p$. (Such sets exist for every prescribed measure in $(0,1)$.) Define
$$U_n=(n,n+1)\setminus C_n,\qquad X_0=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}U_n.$$
Each $U_n$ is open and dense in $(n,n+1)$ with $\lambda(U_n)=p$, so $X_0$ is open and dense in $\mathbb R$ (every open interval meets some $(n,n+1)$ in a non-trivial sub-interval, which in turn meets $U_n$). Moreover
$$\lambda\bigl(X_0\cap[n,n+1]\bigr)=p\quad\text{for every }n,$$
hence $\lambda(X_0\cap[-t,t])=2tp+O(1)$ and consequently
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\lambda(X_0\cap[-t,t])}{2t}=p.$$

**Step 2 — make both sides dense.** The complement $\mathbb R\setminus X_0=\bigcup_n C_n\cup\mathbb Z$ is **not** dense (each $C_n$ is nowhere dense), so we redistribute a countable dense set. Since $X_0$ is open and dense, the set
$$D:=\mathbb Q\cap X_0$$
is countable and dense in $\mathbb R$. Now define
$$X:=X_0\setminus D,\qquad Y:=\mathbb R\setminus X=(\mathbb R\setminus X_0)\cup D.$$
Clearly $X\cup Y=\mathbb R$ and $X\cap Y=\varnothing$.

*Denseness of $X$:* $X_0$ is open and dense; removing the countable set $D$ leaves it dense, since every non-empty open interval meets $X_0$ in an uncountable open set. Hence $X$ is dense in every non-empty open interval.

*Denseness of $Y$:* $Y\supset D$, and $D$ is dense in $\mathbb R$, so $Y$ is dense in every non-empty open interval.

**Step 3 — the densities are unchanged.** Since $D$ is countable, $\lambda(D)=0$, so
$$\lambda(X\cap[-t,t])=\lambda(X_0\cap[-t,t])-\lambda(D\cap[-t,t])=\lambda(X_0\cap[-t,t]).$$
Therefore
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\lambda(X\cap[-t,t])}{2t}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\lambda(X_0\cap[-t,t])}{2t}=p=\frac13.$$
Likewise $\lambda(Y\cap[-t,t])=\lambda((\mathbb R\setminus X_0)\cap[-t,t])$ (again $D$ has measure $0$), giving
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\lambda(Y\cap[-t,t])}{2t}=1-p=\frac23.$$

**Conclusion.** With $p=1/3$ the two limits equal $1/3$ and $2/3$: both are strictly positive and neither equals $1/2$. Thus such a construction exists.
